--- title: "Demo: Point Process Models" subtitle: "FW 532 · Python version" --- This demo has four parts. First we *simulate* presence points from an inhomogeneous Poisson process (IPP). Then we go the other way, as in an SDM: we *fit* a point process model to one simulated pattern, using downweighted Poisson regression. Next we ask how many background (quadrature) points are enough. The second and third parts follow the supplementary material of Renner et al. (2015, Appendix S1, Section 5), and connect to Figure 1 of Valavi et al. (2022). Finally, we use the same trick to fit flexible models (boosted regression trees and Maxent) as point process models, and compare them with a linear GLM on a species with strongly nonlinear responses. You Will Need: numpy, pandas, matplotlib, statsmodels, scikit-learn, elapid, rasterio, and the course helper module `sdmlab.py` (in the same folder as this notebook). Run the cells in order from top to bottom. ::: {#b7cd9605 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Running on Google Colab? This cell downloads the course files. (Anywhere else it does nothing.) import os, sys if "google.colab" in sys.modules: if not os.path.exists("/content/fw532"): !git clone -q --depth 1 https://github.com/Hutchinson-Lab/fw532.git /content/fw532 %pip install -q rasterio elapid os.chdir("/content/fw532/python") ``` ::: # Can we sample from an IPP in Python to understand it better? First, let's go back to our simulation of abundance data, to produce an intensity raster. (The R version of this demo uses the spatstat package to sample point patterns. Python has no direct equivalent, so we write the sampler ourselves below; it takes only a few lines.) ::: {#25fe9d61 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.api as sm import sdmlab as sdm # course helpers for rasters env_stack = sdm.load_env() ``` ::: ::: {#0a9cba9d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # scale variables env_stack = env_stack.scale() intercept = 2 beta1 = 0.5 beta2 = -0.5 beta3 = 0.25 beta4 = -0.05 beta5 = -0.2 mdr = sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Diurnal.Range"]) iso = sdm.scale(env_stack["Isothermality"]) mtwq = sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"]) lambda_map = np.exp(intercept + beta1 * mdr + beta2 * iso + beta3 * mtwq + beta4 * mdr**2 # quadratic term + beta5 * iso * mtwq) # interaction term sdm.plot_map(lambda_map, env_stack, title="lambda"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=526 height=293} ::: ::: ::: {#14f4f6b2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_points = 1000 # any number will work as the seed; using the same one will give the same results sim_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=1234) # could change this from random to a procedure reflecting sampling bias # get the mean abundances that correspond to the points we selected: lambdas = sdm.extract(lambda_map, env_stack, sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"]) # sample from these means (with a *different* seed; see Lab 1): rng = np.random.default_rng(5678) abund = rng.poisson(lam=lambdas) # sampling from a Poisson instead of binomial now # put response and variables together in a DataFrame: abund_df = sim_pts.copy() abund_df.insert(0, "abund", abund) # plot the three relevant climate variables and the mean abundance raster fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5), constrained_layout=True) for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, ["Mean.Diurnal.Range", "Isothermality", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"]): sdm.plot_map(env_stack[name], env_stack, ax=ax, title=name) sdm.plot_map(lambda_map, env_stack, ax=axes[1, 1], title="Mean Abundance"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1066 height=611} ::: ::: Here λ is the mean count at a *site* (a cell). A point process uses the same kind of surface as an *intensity*: the expected number of points per unit area. Under an inhomogeneous Poisson process (IPP), the number of points that land in a cell is Poisson with mean λ × (cell area), so the counts above are what an IPP would give if we measured area in "cells". The number of points an IPP generates is Poisson distributed with mean equal to the integral of the intensity over the whole region, $\Lambda = \int_D \lambda(s)\,ds$. For a raster, the integral is a sum over cells: $\Lambda = \sum_{\text{cells}} \lambda_{\text{cell}} \times (\text{cell area})$. Our cells are 1/6 × 1/6 degree, so each has an area of 1/36 ≈ 0.028 square degrees. (`np.nansum()` adds up the values and skips the `nan` ocean cells.) ::: {#df08ba4f .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} cell_area = env_stack.res**2 # square degrees per cell sum_lambda = np.nansum(lambda_map) print("sum of lambda :", round(sum_lambda, 1)) print("cell area :", round(cell_area, 5), "square degrees") print("expected count :", round(sum_lambda * cell_area, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sum of lambda : 815015.8 cell area : 0.02778 square degrees expected count : 22639.3 ``` ::: ::: So an IPP with this intensity would produce about 22,600 points: enough to crowd the map. Below we divide the intensity by `scale_factor` to get a sparser pattern. **How to sample from an IPP on a raster.** Because λ is constant within each cell, an IPP breaks into independent pieces, one per cell: the number of points in a cell is Poisson with mean λ_cell × (cell area), and those points are spread uniformly at random within the cell. That's all the function below does. (spatstat's `rpoispp()` in R gets the same kind of random pattern by a different route.) ::: {#39d5242d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def sample_ipp(lam, env, rng): """Sample points from an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the map `lam` (expected points per square degree; nan = outside the region).""" mean_counts = np.nan_to_num(lam) * env.res**2 # expected number of points in each cell counts = rng.poisson(mean_counts) # how many points land in each cell row, col = np.nonzero(counts) # the cells that got at least one point n_per_cell = counts[row, col] x_centre, y_centre = env.xy(np.repeat(row, n_per_cell), np.repeat(col, n_per_cell)) n = n_per_cell.sum() # place each point uniformly at random within its cell x = x_centre + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, size=n) * env.res y = y_centre + rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, size=n) * env.res return pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": y}) ``` ::: You can run this cell repeatedly to see samples from the IPP (`default_rng()` with no seed gives new random numbers each time): ::: {#546394d2 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} scale_factor = 25 # Experimenting with scaling. Without dividing, the map is crowded with points. rng = np.random.default_rng() ipp_samp = sample_ipp(lambda_map / scale_factor, env_stack, rng) # sample from the IPP ax = sdm.plot_map(lambda_map / scale_factor, env_stack, cmap="YlGn", title=f"IPP sample with {len(ipp_samp)} points") # plot the (scaled) lambda as a base ax.scatter(ipp_samp["x"], ipp_samp["y"], s=3, color="red"); # add the sampled points on top in red ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=531 height=293} ::: ::: The number of points that are generated is Poisson distributed with mean equal to the integral of the intensity over the entire domain. If you sample a few times, you might believe that the numbers are coming from a Poisson distribution with that mean. Let's check with ten draws (a *list comprehension*, `[... for i in range(10)]`, repeats the expression ten times and collects the results in a list): ::: {#5054e38d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} expected_count = np.nansum(lambda_map / scale_factor) * cell_area counts = [len(sample_ipp(lambda_map / scale_factor, env_stack, rng)) for i in range(10)] print("counts :", counts) print("expected :", round(expected_count, 1)) print("mean of draws:", np.mean(counts), " sd of draws:", round(np.std(counts, ddof=1), 1), " Poisson sd:", round(np.sqrt(expected_count), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` counts : [904, 845, 899, 905, 901, 889, 920, 898, 915, 922] expected : 905.6 mean of draws: 899.8 sd of draws: 21.9 Poisson sd: 30.1 ``` ::: ::: This is why the scaling matters too: dividing λ by `scale_factor` divides the expected count by the same amount. > **The units of area matter.** λ is a rate *per unit area*, so its values only mean something once > the units of area are fixed. If we measured area in pixels (each cell 1 × 1), the expected count > would simply be the *sum* of the cell values (about 815,000 here, before scaling). In square > degrees each cell is 1/36, so the same values give 36 times fewer points. A square degree isn't a > fixed area on the ground, either: it shrinks toward the poles. We might think of a background sample as coming from a homogeneous Poisson process instead. Sampling the entire geographic area regardless of the species intensity. ::: {#0004efaf .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} bkgd_map = np.where(np.isnan(lambda_map), np.nan, 0.3) # You can play with the constant here to see how it changes the number of points bkgd_samp = sample_ipp(bkgd_map, env_stack, rng) ax = sdm.plot_map(bkgd_map, env_stack, cmap="Greys", vmin=0, vmax=1, colorbar=False, title=f"Background sample with {len(bkgd_samp)} points") ax.scatter(bkgd_samp["x"], bkgd_samp["y"], s=3, color="blue"); land_area = np.sum(~np.isnan(lambda_map)) * cell_area print("land area:", round(land_area), "square degrees; expected points:", round(0.3 * land_area)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` land area: 3026 square degrees; expected points: 908 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-2.png){width=566 height=351} ::: ::: For a constant intensity, the integral is just the constant times the area of the region. In Maxent (Lab 6), background points play this role: a sample of the available environments that is used to approximate the integral of λ over the region (Renner et al. 2015). # Fitting a point process model to presence-only data So far we have simulated *from* a point process. An SDM goes the other way: given presence-only records, estimate the intensity. Let's treat one simulated pattern as our presence records. Because we know the true λ, we can check the estimates. ::: {#63dbedc2 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(2468) pres_pts = sample_ipp(lambda_map / scale_factor, env_stack, rng) # our "presence-only records" len(pres_pts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 875 ``` ::: ::: Taking logs of λ (divided by `scale_factor`) gives the true model, a log-linear function of the covariates: $$ \ln \lambda(s) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{MDR} + \beta_2\,\text{Iso} + \beta_3\,\text{MTWQ} + \beta_4\,\text{MDR}^2 + \beta_5\,\text{Iso} \times \text{MTWQ}, $$ with intercept $\beta_0$ = `intercept` − log(`scale_factor`). We'll fit a model of exactly this form, so any differences from the truth come from estimation, not misspecification. ::: {#559b138a .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} true_coefs = pd.Series([intercept - np.log(scale_factor), beta1, beta2, beta3, beta4, beta5], index=["const", "mdr", "iso", "mtwq", "mdr^2", "iso:mtwq"]) def design_matrix(df): """Columns of the model: intercept, the three covariates, the quadratic and the interaction.""" X = df[["mdr", "iso", "mtwq"]].copy() X["mdr^2"] = df["mdr"] ** 2 X["iso:mtwq"] = df["iso"] * df["mtwq"] return sm.add_constant(X) ``` ::: The log-likelihood of an IPP with presence points $s_1, \dots, s_m$ in a region $A$ is $$ \ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \ln \lambda(s_i) \;-\; \int_A \lambda(s)\,ds . $$ The integral has no closed form, so it is approximated by *quadrature*: evaluate λ at a set of quadrature points and add up the values with weights (areas). Quadrature points are what SDM software calls **background points**. Seen this way, background points are not pseudo-absences. They are a device for estimating the integral, so the question to ask about them is how many are needed to estimate it accurately (Renner et al. 2015). We'll come back to that question below. (In R, the spatstat function `ppm()` fits these models directly; the R version of this demo compares it with the approach below.) ## Downweighted Poisson regression (DWPR) Berman & Turner (1992) showed that the quadrature approximation turns the IPP log-likelihood into a weighted Poisson regression, so any GLM software can fit it. Renner et al. (2015, Appendix S1, Section 5.2) gave a simple recipe, *downweighted Poisson regression*. Take the $m$ presence points and $n$ quadrature points drawn at random from the region. Then: * give each **quadrature point** weight $w = |A|/n$ (its share of the region's area) and response $z = 0$; * give each **presence point** a tiny weight $w = \epsilon$ and response $z = 1/\epsilon$; * fit a Poisson GLM of $z$ with these weights. The weighted Poisson log-likelihood, $\sum_k w_k (z_k \ln \mu_k - \mu_k)$, is then $$ \sum_{i=1}^{m} \ln \lambda(s_i) \;-\; \frac{|A|}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} \lambda(q_j) \;-\; \underbrace{\epsilon \sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda(s_i)}_{\approx\, 0}, $$ which is the IPP log-likelihood, with the integral estimated as |A| × (average of λ over the quadrature points). In statsmodels the weights go in `var_weights=`, which plays the role of the `weights=` argument of R's `glm()`. The quadrature points are drawn from the region's grid cells, so first we make a table of every cell and its covariate values: ::: {#e02621b6 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} row, col = np.nonzero(~np.isnan(lambda_map)) # every cell in the region all_cells = pd.DataFrame({"mdr": mdr[row, col], "iso": iso[row, col], "mtwq": mtwq[row, col]}) region_area = len(all_cells) * cell_area # |A|, in square degrees pres_covs = pd.DataFrame({name: sdm.extract(m, env_stack, pres_pts["x"], pres_pts["y"]) for name, m in [("mdr", mdr), ("iso", iso), ("mtwq", mtwq)]}) def dwpr_data(quad_pts, pres_df=None, eps=1e-6): """Presences + quadrature points, with DWPR weights (wt) and response (z).""" if pres_df is None: pres_df = pres_covs # covariates at the presences of our first species dat = pd.concat([pres_df.assign(pres=1), quad_pts[["mdr", "iso", "mtwq"]].assign(pres=0)], ignore_index=True) dat["wt"] = np.where(dat["pres"] == 1, eps, region_area / len(quad_pts)) # quadrature weights dat["z"] = dat["pres"] / dat["wt"] # 1/eps at presences, 0 elsewhere return dat def fit_dwpr(quad_pts, eps=1e-6): """Fit an IPP by downweighted Poisson regression (Renner et al. 2015, Appendix S1, Section 5.2).""" dat = dwpr_data(quad_pts, eps=eps) wt, z = dat["wt"].to_numpy(), dat["z"].to_numpy() fit = sm.GLM(z, design_matrix(dat), family=sm.families.Poisson(), var_weights=wt).fit() mu = fit.fittedvalues.to_numpy() return {"fit": fit, "loglik": np.sum(wt * (z * np.log(mu) - mu)), # the IPP log-likelihood "quad_intensity": mu[dat["pres"].to_numpy() == 0]} # fitted intensity at quadrature points ``` ::: Let's fit it with 10,000 random quadrature points, Maxent's default number of background points: ::: {#f0014d6b .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(1357) quad_10k = all_cells.iloc[rng.choice(len(all_cells), size=10000, replace=False)] dwpr_10k = fit_dwpr(quad_10k) pd.DataFrame({"truth": true_coefs, "DWPR": dwpr_10k["fit"].params, "SE": dwpr_10k["fit"].bse}).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
truth DWPR SE
const -1.219 -1.242 0.048
mdr 0.500 0.459 0.080
iso -0.500 -0.384 0.087
mtwq 0.250 0.203 0.053
mdr^2 -0.050 -0.019 0.031
iso:mtwq -0.200 -0.229 0.068
``` ::: ::: The estimates land close to the true coefficients, mostly within about two standard errors. Unlike presence–background logistic regression, DWPR estimates the intercept on the scale of the intensity (points per square degree), so its fitted values are a proper intensity map: ::: {#3c1fa740 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} pred = dwpr_10k["fit"].predict(design_matrix(all_cells)) pred_map = np.full(lambda_map.shape, np.nan) pred_map[row, col] = pred # put the predictions back on the grid fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), constrained_layout=True) vmax = np.nanmax(pred_map) sdm.plot_map(lambda_map / scale_factor, env_stack, ax=axes[0], title="True intensity", vmin=0, vmax=vmax) sdm.plot_map(pred_map, env_stack, ax=axes[1], title="DWPR estimate", vmin=0, vmax=vmax); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1162 height=322} ::: ::: > **The link to logistic regression and Maxent (IWLR).** Fithian & Hastie (2013) showed that a > logistic regression of presences against background points, with a huge weight $W$ on the > background points, recovers the same slopes. This is *infinitely weighted logistic regression* > (IWLR). It is how `elapid` and R's `maxnet` fit Maxent, with $W = 100$ (Lab 6). The intercept, > though, is arbitrary: it is shifted by log(W·n/|A|). That's why Maxent's raw output is only > *proportional* to the intensity (Appendix S1, Section 5.1). ::: {#8de06838 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} dat = pd.concat([pres_covs.assign(pres=1), quad_10k.assign(pres=0)], ignore_index=True) w_iwlr = (1e6) ** (1 - dat["pres"]) # W = 10^6 on background points, 1 on presences fit_iwlr = sm.GLM(dat["pres"], design_matrix(dat), family=sm.families.Binomial(), var_weights=w_iwlr).fit() print(pd.DataFrame({"IWLR": fit_iwlr.params, "DWPR": dwpr_10k["fit"].params}).round(3)) print("intercept gap:", round(dwpr_10k["fit"].params["const"] - fit_iwlr.params["const"], 4), " log(W n / |A|):", round(np.log(1e6 * len(quad_10k) / region_area), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` IWLR DWPR const -16.253 -1.242 mdr 0.459 0.459 iso -0.384 -0.384 mtwq 0.203 0.203 mdr^2 -0.019 -0.019 iso:mtwq -0.229 -0.229 intercept gap: 15.0109 log(W n / |A|): 15.0109 ``` ::: ::: > **What the intercept can't tell you: records vs. individuals.** Think of λ as the species' > abundance (individuals per square degree), with only 1 in `scale_factor` = 25 individuals becoming > a record. The records then follow an IPP with intensity λ/25, and that is what the model > estimates. The fitted intercept is close to `intercept` − log(25), and the slopes don't depend on > `scale_factor` at all. With real data the 25 is unknown. It mixes how abundant the species is with > how hard people looked, so presence records alone can't tell a rare, well-surveyed species from a > common, poorly surveyed one. Phillips et al. (2017) call this unknown ratio of true abundance to > the model's estimate *c*. > > That matters as soon as you want a probability of presence. If individuals occur independently, > the number in a cell of area *a* is Poisson with mean *a*·*c*·λ̂, where λ̂ is the fitted > intensity. So the probability that the species is present is 1 − exp(−*a*·*c*·λ̂). Without *c*, > the same formula only gives the probability that a cell holds at least one *record*: ::: {#f27b18d4 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} p_record = 1 - np.exp(-cell_area * pred_map) # at least one record in the cell p_present = 1 - np.exp(-cell_area * scale_factor * pred_map) # species present: needs c = scale_factor fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), constrained_layout=True) sdm.plot_map(p_record, env_stack, ax=axes[0], title="P(at least one record)", vmin=0, vmax=1) sdm.plot_map(p_present, env_stack, ax=axes[1], title="P(present), if we knew c = 25", vmin=0, vmax=1); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=1162 height=322} ::: ::: > This isn't about the units of area: switching from square degrees to km² changes *a* and λ̂ in > opposite directions and leaves *a*·λ̂ unchanged. Maxent's cloglog output (Lab 6) uses the same > formula, but replaces the unknown *c*, *a*, and intercept with a constant based on the model's > entropy. So it is a probability of presence in a quadrat whose size depends on the unknown *c* > (Phillips et al. 2017). > > That's a different problem from the "scale dependence" described by Renner & Warton (2013), where > Maxent's intercept and predicted probabilities change with the spatial resolution or the number of > background points. DWPR's area weights fix that problem. No choice of weights fixes this one: > estimating *c* needs information beyond the presence records, such as presence–absence surveys or > an estimate of total population size. # Are there enough background points? Every number above depends on the integral being estimated well. With too few quadrature points, the log-likelihood (and so the coefficients, standard errors, and model comparisons) carry extra error that has nothing to do with the species. Renner et al. (2015) suggest two ways to check. ## Check 1: does the log-likelihood settle down? Refit the model with more and more random quadrature points and see where the maximized log-likelihood stops changing (Appendix S1, Section 5.3; Renner et al. 2015, Fig. 2b). Because the points are random, we repeat each size several times to see how much the answer varies from one set of quadrature points to another. We also have a reference value. Our covariates are constant within each grid cell, so using *every* cell as a quadrature point (weight = one cell's area) computes the integral exactly at the resolution of our data. ::: {#44968987 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} dwpr_all = fit_dwpr(all_cells) # every cell: the exact integral at this resolution n_quad = [500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000] n_reps = 20 rng = np.random.default_rng(8642) log_liks = np.array([[fit_dwpr(all_cells.iloc[rng.choice(len(all_cells), size=n, replace=False)])["loglik"] for n in n_quad] for rep in range(n_reps)]) # n_reps rows x len(n_quad) columns fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) for j, n in enumerate(n_quad): ax.scatter(np.full(n_reps, n), log_liks[:, j], s=15, color="black", alpha=0.4) ax.axhline(dwpr_all["loglik"], color="red", linestyle="--", label="all cells (exact)") ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_xticks(n_quad, [f"{n:,}" for n in n_quad]) # label the sizes we used ax.minorticks_off() ax.set_xlabel("Number of random quadrature points (log scale)") ax.set_ylabel("Maximized log-likelihood") ax.set_title(f"{n_reps} random sets of quadrature points at each size") ax.legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=688 height=414} ::: ::: With a few hundred quadrature points, the log-likelihood can be off by tens of units, depending only on which points were drawn. The spread narrows as $n$ grows. This is the same check as Figure 1 of Valavi et al. (2022), the model benchmark we read in Week 6. Before choosing the number of background points for their study, they refitted MaxEnt with 100 to 100,000 random background points, repeating each size 10 times. They compared the results with a "gold standard" model that used every cell in the landscape as background, just like our all-cells reference line. Their yardstick was predictive performance (test AUC) rather than the log-likelihood; Renner et al. (2015) suggest either. Valavi et al. chose 50,000 background points, the size at which the replicates came close to the gold standard. ## Check 2: the standard error of the integral Renner et al. (2015, p. 370) point out that this spread can be predicted with a familiar formula. With $n$ random quadrature points, the integral is estimated as |A| times the *average* fitted intensity at those points. That's a sample mean, so its standard error is the usual one: $$ \text{SE}(n) = \frac{|A|\, s}{\sqrt{n}}, $$ where $s$ is the standard deviation of the fitted intensity across the region, estimated from the quadrature points of an initial fit. Turned around, this tells us how many points we need. If we want the SE to be at most some tolerance $\tau$ (in log-likelihood units), we need $$ n \;\ge\; \left(\frac{|A|\, s}{\tau}\right)^2 . $$ Renner et al. used $\tau = 2$. That is a sensible scale: differences of a couple of log-likelihood units are what decide model comparisons. For example, a likelihood-ratio test for one extra term at the 5% level needs a difference of 1.92. ::: {#28dad9d9 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = np.std(dwpr_10k["quad_intensity"], ddof=1) # spread of the fitted intensity, from the 10,000-point fit def se_loglik(n): return region_area * s / np.sqrt(n) tolerance = 2 n_required = int(np.ceil((region_area * s / tolerance) ** 2)) print("s :", round(s, 3)) print("SE with 10,000 points:", round(se_loglik(10000), 2)) print("n required (SE <= 2) :", n_required) print("cells in the region :", len(all_cells)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` s : 0.135 SE with 10,000 points: 4.08 n required (SE <= 2) : 41614 cells in the region : 108932 ``` ::: ::: How well does the formula predict the simulation? Compare the standard deviation of the 20 log-likelihoods at each size with SE(n): ::: {#fbccf6fd .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({"simulated SD": log_liks.std(axis=0, ddof=1), "formula SE": se_loglik(np.array(n_quad))}, index=pd.Index(n_quad, name="n")).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}

(With only 20 replicates, the simulated standard deviations are themselves noisy, by roughly ±15%.) So one quick initial fit tells us roughly how many background points are needed, without running all the replicates. For this species the rule's answer (printed above) is the same order as the 50,000 points that Valavi et al. (2022) settled on by the slower, replicate-based route. At the largest sizes the simulated spread is a bit *smaller* than the formula predicts. That's because we are sampling without replacement from a finite set of cells: with half of all cells in the sample, the SE shrinks by a factor of about $\sqrt{1 - n/N}$, and with every cell the integral is exact. ## How much does it matter for the coefficients? The log-likelihood matters for comparing models. What about the coefficients themselves? Here is how much they vary across random sets of quadrature points, next to their usual (model-based) standard errors: ::: {#9bb1b842 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(9753) coef_sd = {"model SE": dwpr_all["fit"].bse} for n in [1000, 10000, 50000]: coefs = pd.DataFrame([fit_dwpr(all_cells.iloc[rng.choice(len(all_cells), size=n, replace=False)])["fit"].params for rep in range(n_reps)]) coef_sd[f"quadrature SD, n={n}"] = coefs.std(ddof=1) pd.DataFrame(coef_sd).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}

(2015, Fig. 2a) checked convergence > with a grid of decreasing spacing. # Beyond GLMs: flexible models as point process models DWPR turns fitting a point process model into fitting a weighted Poisson regression. So any method that can fit a Poisson model with observation weights can fit a point process model, not just GLMs. Renner et al. (2015) make this point for DWPR, and Fithian & Hastie (2013) make the same point for weighted logistic regression. Two flexible methods from this course qualify: * **Boosted regression trees.** A Poisson BRT can take exactly the same response `z` and weights `wt` as the GLM. The trees learn the shapes of the responses and any interactions from the data, and the model still estimates the intensity on its true scale. * **Maxent.** `elapid` (like R's `maxnet`) fits Maxent by infinitely weighted logistic regression (see the IWLR note above). It expands each covariate into many features (linear, quadratic, product, hinge) and uses L1 regularization to keep only the ones that help (Lab 6). Using point-process weights for BRTs is not the usual practice. In their benchmark, Valavi et al. (2022) fitted BRTs as presence-vs-background *classifiers* (Bernoulli loss), with the background points down-weighted so that their total weight equals that of the presences. That is the approach Renner et al. (2015) call statistically naïve. Valavi et al. used point-process weighting only for GLMs and GAMs. Our first species is a poor test of flexible methods, though. Its true intensity has a quadratic term and an interaction, but the GLM we fitted contained *exactly* those terms: it was told the true formula. Those effects were also mild. In a real analysis nobody tells you the form. So let's simulate a second species whose responses a simple GLM can't represent, and compare three models that are *not* told the form: a linear GLM, a Poisson BRT, and Maxent. ## A species with nonlinear responses Species 2 has a hump-shaped response to mean diurnal range (an optimum near its average), a sharp threshold in the temperature of the wettest quarter, and a steady decline with isothermality: $$ \ln \lambda_2(s) = \alpha_2 - 0.8\,\text{MDR}^2 + 1.5 \cdot \mathbb{1}[\text{MTWQ} > 0] - 0.5\,\text{Iso}, $$ where $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ is 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise. We pick $\alpha_2$ so that about 900 points are expected. ::: {#da3b66a6 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} def shape2(d): """Species 2's log intensity, minus its intercept: hump + step + linear.""" return -0.8 * d["mdr"] ** 2 + 1.5 * (d["mtwq"] > 0) - 0.5 * d["iso"] alpha2 = np.log(900 / (np.sum(np.exp(shape2(all_cells))) * cell_area)) # gives ~900 expected points lambda2_map = np.full(lambda_map.shape, np.nan) lambda2_map[row, col] = np.exp(alpha2 + shape2(all_cells)) # the true intensity map rng = np.random.default_rng(4321) pres_pts2 = sample_ipp(lambda2_map, env_stack, rng) # training "presence records" rng = np.random.default_rng(5555) test_pts2 = sample_ipp(lambda2_map, env_stack, rng) # an independent test pattern from the same process def covariates_at(pts): """The three covariates at a set of points.""" return pd.DataFrame({name: sdm.extract(m, env_stack, pts["x"], pts["y"]) for name, m in [("mdr", mdr), ("iso", iso), ("mtwq", mtwq)]}) pres_covs2 = covariates_at(pres_pts2) test_covs2 = covariates_at(test_pts2) print("training points:", len(pres_covs2), " test points:", len(test_covs2)) ax = sdm.plot_map(lambda2_map, env_stack, title="True intensity of species 2, with its training points") ax.scatter(pres_pts2["x"], pres_pts2["y"], s=2, color="red"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` training points: 861 test points: 889 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-23-output-2.png){width=531 height=293} ::: ::: ## Fitting the three models All three models get the same 50,000 random quadrature (background) points. That's the number Valavi et al. (2022) chose, and close to what the standard-error rule asked for with species 1. (Checking it for species 2 is one of the questions below.) ::: {#aef75b32 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(6666) quad2 = all_cells.iloc[rng.choice(len(all_cells), size=50000, replace=False)] dat2 = dwpr_data(quad2, pres_df=pres_covs2) # DWPR response (z) and weights (wt) for species 2 covs = ["mdr", "iso", "mtwq"] ``` ::: **A linear GLM** (DWPR), the simplest model you might try without knowing the form: ::: {#b7766ab2 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit_linear = sm.GLM(dat2["z"], sm.add_constant(dat2[covs]), family=sm.families.Poisson(), var_weights=dat2["wt"]).fit() ``` ::: **A Poisson BRT** with the same response and weights. In R this is the gbm package with `distribution = "poisson"` and `weights =`. In scikit-learn, `GradientBoostingClassifier` (Lab 5) has no Poisson loss, but `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` does (`loss="poisson"`), and it accepts weights through `sample_weight=`. It first bins each covariate into at most 255 values, which makes it fast. Settings map roughly to gbm's: `learning_rate` is the shrinkage, and `max_leaf_nodes=3` gives two-split trees like gbm's `interaction.depth = 2`. Instead of cross-validation, we let it stop adding trees when the loss on a held-out 20% of the data stops improving (*early stopping*). ::: {#c7288961 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor fit_brt = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="poisson", learning_rate=0.02, max_leaf_nodes=3, max_iter=3000, early_stopping=True, validation_fraction=0.2, n_iter_no_change=50, random_state=0) fit_brt.fit(dat2[covs], dat2["z"], sample_weight=dat2["wt"]) print("number of trees chosen by early stopping:", fit_brt.n_iter_) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` number of trees chosen by early stopping: 357 ``` ::: ::: **Maxent** with `elapid`, given the presences and the same quadrature points as background. We use the same feature classes as maxnet's defaults (for more than 80 presences) and a regularization multiplier of 1. We also ask for 50 hinge features per covariate, as maxnet uses. elapid's default of 10 is noticeably less flexible here. `transform="raw"` makes `predict()` return a value proportional to exp(linear predictor). ::: {#6412535d .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} import elapid fit_maxent = elapid.MaxentModel(feature_types=["linear", "quadratic", "product", "hinge"], beta_multiplier=1.0, n_hinge_features=50, transform="raw") fit_maxent.fit(dat2[covs], dat2["pres"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``````{=html}

`````` ::: ::: Maxent's output is only *proportional* to the intensity, because the IWLR intercept is arbitrary. For a Poisson point process, the maximum-likelihood intercept makes the expected number of points, $\int_A \lambda(s)\,ds$, equal the number observed. So we rescale Maxent's output to make its integral, estimated with the same quadrature points, equal to the number of presences: ::: {#355f10e0 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} maxent_scale = len(pres_covs2) / (region_area * fit_maxent.predict(quad2[covs]).mean()) def maxent_intensity(d): return maxent_scale * fit_maxent.predict(d[covs]) ``` ::: ## Comparing the models First, the test log-likelihood of each model on the independent test pattern (with the integral computed exactly over every cell), with the truth and a constant intensity for reference: ::: {#de318e6c .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} def test_loglik(intensity, test_covs): """IPP log-likelihood of the test points, for a function that returns the fitted intensity.""" return np.sum(np.log(intensity(test_covs))) - np.sum(intensity(all_cells)) * cell_area pd.Series({ "truth": test_loglik(lambda d: np.exp(alpha2 + shape2(d)), test_covs2), "linear GLM": test_loglik(lambda d: fit_linear.predict(sm.add_constant(d[covs])), test_covs2), "BRT": test_loglik(lambda d: fit_brt.predict(d[covs]), test_covs2), "Maxent": test_loglik(maxent_intensity, test_covs2), "constant": test_loglik(lambda d: np.full(len(d), len(pres_covs2) / region_area), test_covs2), }, name="test log-likelihood").round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` truth -1570.6 linear GLM -1773.0 BRT -1591.4 Maxent -1599.0 constant -1978.4 Name: test log-likelihood, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: (A `lambda` is a small unnamed function, so `lambda d: ...` means "a function of `d` that returns ...". Each one here returns a model's fitted intensity for a table of covariates.) The maps, on a common color scale capped at the true maximum (`imshow` colors higher values with the top color): ::: {#480da5d2 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} pred_maps = {"Truth": lambda2_map} for name, intensity in [("Linear GLM (DWPR)", lambda d: fit_linear.predict(sm.add_constant(d[covs]))), ("BRT (Poisson, DWPR weights)", lambda d: fit_brt.predict(d[covs])), ("Maxent (elapid)", maxent_intensity)]: m = np.full(lambda_map.shape, np.nan) m[row, col] = intensity(all_cells) pred_maps[name] = m fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7.5), constrained_layout=True) for ax, (name, m) in zip(axes.flat, pred_maps.items()): sdm.plot_map(m, env_stack, ax=ax, title=name, vmin=0, vmax=np.nanmax(lambda2_map)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-30-output-1.png){width=1258 height=708} ::: ::: And the response curves: each model's log intensity as one covariate varies, with the other two held at 0 (their average). The models differ in their overall level, so we center each curve (subtract its mean) to compare *shapes*: ::: {#fd384588 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} log_intensity = { "truth": lambda d: alpha2 + shape2(d), "linear GLM": lambda d: np.log(fit_linear.predict(sm.add_constant(d[covs], has_constant="add"))), "BRT": lambda d: np.log(fit_brt.predict(d[covs])), "Maxent": lambda d: np.log(fit_maxent.predict(d[covs])), } styles = {"truth": ("black", "--"), "linear GLM": ("orange", "-"), "BRT": ("forestgreen", "-"), "Maxent": ("purple", "-")} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4), constrained_layout=True) for ax, v in zip(axes, ["mdr", "mtwq", "iso"]): sweep = pd.DataFrame({"mdr": np.zeros(200), "iso": 0.0, "mtwq": 0.0}) # others held at 0 sweep[v] = np.linspace(all_cells[v].quantile(0.01), all_cells[v].quantile(0.99), 200) for name, f in log_intensity.items(): curve = np.asarray(f(sweep), dtype=float) color, linestyle = styles[name] ax.plot(sweep[v], curve - curve.mean(), color=color, linestyle=linestyle, lw=2, label=name) ax.set_xlabel(v) ax.set_ylabel("log intensity (centered)") ax.set_title(v) axes[0].legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](demo-point-processes_files/figure-html/cell-31-output-1.png){width=1355 height=395} ::: ::: The linear GLM can't bend: it draws a nearly flat line through the hump and a tilted line through the step. Its test log-likelihood is far below the truth's, though still well above a constant intensity. Both flexible models recover the shapes and come much closer to the truth, and close to each other. Their curves show their characters. Maxent's quadratic features capture the hump smoothly, and its hinges trace the step. The BRT captures the step crisply but draws everything as small stairs, and it goes flat beyond the data. This isn't a contest with a fixed winner: a different species, or more careful tuning of either model, could reverse their order. > **Questions** > > * Why do the BRT and Maxent need just as many quadrature points as the GLM?
